How to choose tyre pressure for city riding

26

By Lea Hartmann · 3 March 2026

27 28

The number printed on the tyre sidewall is a maximum, not a recommendation. On cobbles and patched asphalt, most riders are faster and more comfortable a good way below it.

29 30

Start from the tyre width

31 32

As a starting point for a rider of about 75 kg: 28 mm tyres at 5 to 5.5 bar, 35 mm tyres at 3.5 to 4 bar, and 47 mm tyres at 2.5 to 3 bar. Put about 0.3 bar less in the front than in the rear.

33 34

Then adjust by feel

35

If the bike bounces over cobbles, let some air out. If the tyre squirms in corners or you feel the rim hit an edge, add some. Check the pressure every two weeks: tyres lose air slowly even without a puncture.

Winter chain care: keep your drivetrain running through the salt season

26

By Jonas Albrecht · 18 November 2025 · Print version

27 28

Every January we replace more chains than in the rest of the year together. Road salt and wet grit turn a chain into sandpaper, and a worn chain then wears out the cassette and chainrings as well. Ten minutes a week keeps most of that away.

29 30

Clean it, do not drown it

31 32

Wipe the chain with a dry rag while you turn the cranks backwards. If it is very dirty, use a little degreaser on the rag, not a jet of water: a pressure washer pushes water past the seals into the bearings.

33 34

Use a wet lube or wax, and wipe off the extra

35 36

In winter a wet lube lasts longer between rain rides. Put one drop on each roller, turn the cranks for a minute, and then wipe the outside of the chain. Lube that stays on the outside only collects dirt.

37 38

Measure wear once a month

39

A chain checker costs a few euros. When it shows 0.5 % wear on an 11- or 12-speed chain, or 0.75 % on a chain with fewer gears, change the chain before it damages the cassette.

40 41

If you would rather leave it to us, the chain is checked and cleaned in every service – see our repair prices.

content.text:
Full picture now. Here's what's actually keeping the site out of Google, roughly in order of impact:

1. **`services.html` (the pricing page) has `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">`** — Google is explicitly told not to index your main commercial page and not to follow any links on it. This alone can explain most of the "barely shows up" problem.
2. **`robots.txt` blocks `/blog/` entirely**, even though the blog has real posts, is linked from the homepage, and is listed in the sitemap. Blocking it throws away exactly the long-tail content ("tyre pressure city riding", "winter chain care") that ranks small local shops on Google.
3. **The "Shop" nav link isn't a real link** — it's a `<span onclick="...">` on every single page, not an `<a href>`. Search engines primarily discover pages by following `<a href>` links, so `/shop/` and its product page are effectively undiscoverable through navigation.
4. **Broken hreflang (EN↔DE) annotations**: `contact.html`/`de/kontakt.html` use the invalid language code `ge` instead of `de`, and `de/leistungen.html` has no link back to the English `services.html` at all — hreflang pairs must point both ways or Google ignores them, which undermines your EN/DE targeting specifically.
5. Smaller stuff: a duplicated/contradictory `<link rel="canonical">` on the shop product page, a canonical URL using `http://` instead of `https://` on one blog post, three internal/sitemap links pointing to a nonexistent `/repairs.html` (404), and a noindexed page listed in the sitemap.

I'll fix all of these now, plus add local-business structured data so Google can show your address/hours/phone directly in results — this uses only facts already on your site.

## Summary

Your site had several things actively telling Google *not* to show it — this wasn't really a "not found" problem, it was a "told not to look" problem:

**Fixed:**
- **`services.html` had `noindex, nofollow`** — your pricing page, arguably your most important page, was invisible to Google and blocked from passing links to `/contact.html`. Removed.
- **`de/index.html`'s canonical tag pointed at the English homepage** instead of itself — this told Google the German homepage wasn't a real, distinct page, which would suppress it from German results specifically. Fixed to self-reference `/de/`.
- **`robots.txt` blocked `/blog/` entirely** while the sitemap and homepage linked to real posts inside it. Unblocked.
- **The "Shop" link was JavaScript (`onclick`), not a real `<a href>`**, on all 12 pages — crawlers can miss those, so `/shop/` and its product page were poorly discoverable. Converted to real links everywhere.
- **Broken EN↔DE hreflang**: `contact.html`/`de/kontakt.html` used the invalid code `ge` instead of `de`; `de/leistungen.html` didn't link back to `services.html` at all. Both pairs are now correct and reciprocal, with `x-default` added for consistency.
- Cleanup: duplicate/contradictory canonical tag on the shop product page, an `http://` canonical on one blog post, three dead links to a nonexistent `/repairs.html`, and a noindexed page that was listed in the sitemap.
- **Added `BicycleStore` structured data** (name, address, phone, hours) to both homepages, using only facts already published on the site — this helps Google show your address/hours directly in results and improves local-search matching.

**Not code fixes, but worth knowing:** a lot of "found on Google for a local shop" comes from outside the HTML — a claimed, complete **Google Business Profile** (with the exact same NAP — name/address/phone — as the site) and a few genuine customer reviews there typically move the needle for local search more than anything on-page. I didn't touch that since it's an account action, not a file change.

One thing to flag before you publish: all URLs on the site use the placeholder domain `werkbankcycles.example` — make sure your real domain is swapped in everywhere (canonical, hreflang, sitemap, robots.txt) once you deploy, or these tags will point at the wrong place.
